children.text: The nomenclature of complexes follows a system proposed by Swiss chemist and Nobel laureate Alfred Werner, who laid the foundation for understanding coordination compounds more than a century ago. Although naming customs vary, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) recommends the following naming system for precise chemical communication among scientists. Here are five basic rules for naming transition metal compounds and complexes:
For ionic coordination compounds, follow the standard naming rules: cation first, anion second.
Name the ligands first, followed by the central metal atom. Name the ligands alphabetically.

For most neutral ligands, the name of the molecule is used. The four common exceptions are
If more than one ligand of a given type is present, the number is indicated by a Greek prefix.

Special prefixes are used when the ligand name includes Greek prefixes (such as "di" in ethylenediamine) and for polydentate ligands in general. When a special prefix is used, the name of the ligand it refers to is put in parentheses.
How the metal ion is named depends on the type of complex or compound.
When the complex is a cation or a neutral molecule, the name of the central metal atom is spelled like the element and is followed by a Roman numeral in parentheses to indicate its oxidation state.
When the complex is an anion, the suffix -ate is added to the stem of the name of the metal, followed by the Roman numeral designation of its oxidation state.

Writing the chemical formula from the name or structure of a coordination complex or compound applies the same nomenclature rules, just in reverse.  Many people find writing the formula from a provided name to be easier.
